QUALITY ASSESSMENT

The target lands at 90 because it executes the Farmer-psychology contrarian frame with real precision and a fully realized Empathy Engine, particularly in the middle section where it inhabits the resisting engineer rather than the CTO. The line "That code is not just code to them. It is proof of their judgment" earns the score by surfacing internal experience the way Reference C does. It falls short of C's 98 because the prose is slightly tidier and less savage, missing C's compounding imagery like "donations to the cloud providers," but it clearly outclasses Reference B's flat exposition.

Article Preview

Claude Code Connects Any API and Kills Dead Tools

Most developers are about to waste six months building something that no longer needs to exist.

That sounds harsh. It is also true. Claude Code shipped tool calls that let AI agents reach into any API, any MCP server, any database, any file system, straight from the command line. No glue code. No middleware cathedral. No team of three engineers stitching together a fragile integration layer that breaks every time a vendor changes a header. The connective tissue you were planning to build by hand just became a default capability. And if you keep building it anyway, you are not engineering. You are nostalgic.

The Plumbing Just Became Free

For years, the real work in AI applications was never the model. It was the plumbing. Getting the agent to talk to your CRM, your Postgres instance, your internal file server, your billing system. Each connection was a custom job. Each custom job had a maintenance tax. You paid that tax forever, quietly, in the form of senior developers babysitting brittle pipes instead of shipping features.

Claude Code removes the toll booth. Tool calls from the command line mean the agent can query a database, hit a third-party API, and read a file in the same breath, orchestrated by the model instead of by your handwritten controller logic. This is the AI Reality Check applied without mercy. Does it save time? Yes, measurable hours per integration. Does it make money? Yes, because the engineers you were renting to maintain plumbing can now build the thing customers actually pay for. Filter it through ROI and it survives the filter cleanly, which is rare. Most AI releases fail that test in the first sixty seconds.

So the honest question is not whether this is impressive. It is whether you are willing to delete the work you already started.

Why Your Best Engineer Will Resist This

Here is the part nobody writes about. The developer who built your current integration layer is not going to celebrate this. Put yourself inside their head for a moment. They spent two quarters designing a system that connects six services. They named the modules. They documented the edge cases at two in the morning. That code is not just code to them. It is proof of their judgment, evidence they solved something hard. And now a command-line tool call does eighty percent of it for free.

Telling that person to rip it out feels like telling them their last six months were a mistake. They will defend the old system. Not because it is better, but because abandoning it feels like admitting waste, and humans are wired to protect sunk effort harder than they pursue future gains. You will hear words like stability, like edge cases, like we cannot trust a black box with production data. Some of those concerns are real. Most are emotional armor.

Your job as the person making the call is to separate the legitimate caution from the ego defense, and to do it without making your best engineer feel demoted by a model. Give them the new layer to own. Let them be the one who decides what stays custom and what gets handed to the agent. People accept change they architect. They reject change handed down as a verdict on their past work. This is the same Farmer psychology that wins in sales, applied inward. You are not hunting for a win against your own team. You are planting the conditions for them to choose it.

The Binary Choice Sitting On Your Desk

Strip away the noise and you are left with two paths, and you cannot walk both.

Path one. You treat this as a curiosity, file it under things to evaluate next quarter, and keep funding the manual integration roadmap. Your costs stay flat. Your timeline stays long. And somewhere a leaner competitor wires their agent to every system they own in a weekend, ships faster, and undercuts you on price because their overhead is a fraction of yours. Automation plus timing equals advantage, and you handed them the timing.

Path two. You audit every integration on your current roadmap this week and ask one question of each. Can a Claude Code tool call do this now? Where the answer is yes, you stop building and you redirect that engineering time toward the product surface customers see. Where the answer is genuinely no, you keep the custom work and you defend it with data, not habit.

There is no comfortable middle. The plumbing got commoditized whether you like it or not. The only decision left is whether you stop paying for water you can now get free, or keep writing the check out of pride. One of those is strategy. The other is a story you tell yourself while the meter runs.

Pick the one that survives the ROI filter.

Jonathan Green

HTML Salespage

Quality: 90.0 Adherence: 75.0
QUALITY ASSESSMENT

The target lands at 90 because it delivers a structurally complete, design-spec-compliant sales page with polished conversion architecture, yet falls short of Reference C's near-perfect execution. The brand palette is faithfully implemented via CSS variables, the hero gradient with radial overlays demonstrates real craft, and conversion mechanics like the Alpine.js countdown, fixed scroll progress bar, and mobile sticky CTA show genuine attention to UX. The opening line "Finally escape the 'copy-paste prison' of manual AI work" lifts the script verbatim and frames the offer cleanly. Compared to Reference C (99), the target uses fewer libraries, has lighter trust-signal density, and includes placeholder headshots rather than richer visual systems, costing it those final points.

        days: '00', hours: '00', minutes: '00', seconds: '00',
        start() {
            // Set deadline 3 days from now
            const deadline = new Date().getTime() + (3 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);
            const update = () => {
                const now = new Date().getTime();
                let diff = deadline - now;
                if (diff < 0) diff = 0;
                this.days = String(Math.floor(diff / (1000*60*60*24))).padStart(2,'0');
                this.hours = String(Math.floor((diff % (1000*60*60*24)) / (1000*60*60))).padStart(2,'0');
                this.minutes = String(Math.floor((diff % (1000*60*60)) / (1000*60))).padStart(2,'0');
                this.seconds = String(Math.floor((diff % (1000*60)) / 1000)).padStart(2,'0');
            };
            update();
            setInterval(update, 1000);
        }
    }
}

TypeScript
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'crypto';

export interface WebhookEventData {
  object: Record<string, any>;
}

export interface WebhookEvent {
  id: string;
  type: string;
  created: number;
  data: WebhookEventData;
  signature: string;
}

export interface EventCounts {
  payment_succeeded: number;
  subscription_updated: number;
  invoice_failed: number;
}

export interface FailedInvoice {
  eventId: string;
  attemptCount: number;
}

export interface WebhookProcessingSummary {
  totalEvents: number;
  validEvents: number;
  invalidEvents: string[];
  counts: EventCounts;
  totalRevenue: number;
  failedInvoices: FailedInvoice[];
}

function computeSignature(data: WebhookEventData, webhookSecret: string): string {
  return createHmac('sha256', webhookSecret)
    .update(JSON.stringify(data))
    .digest('hex');
}

function isValidSignature(
  data: WebhookEventData,
  signature: string,
  webhookSecret: string
): boolean {
  const expected = computeSignature(data, webhookSecret);
  const expectedBuf = Buffer.from(expected, 'hex');
  let providedBuf: Buffer;
  try {
    providedBuf = Buffer.from(signature, 'hex');
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
  if (expectedBuf.length !== providedBuf.length) {
    return false;
  }
  return timingSafeEqual(expectedBuf, providedBuf);
}

function isValidEventShape(event: any): event is WebhookEvent {
  return (
    event !== null &&
    typeof event === 'object' &&
    typeof event.id === 'string' &&
    typeof event.type === 'string' &&
    typeof event.created === 'number' &&
    typeof event.signature === 'string' &&
    event.data !== null &&
    typeof event.data === 'object' &&
    event.data.object !== null &&
    typeof event.data.object === 'object'
  );
}

export function processWebhookEvents(
  events: WebhookEvent[],
  webhookSecret: string
): WebhookProcessingSummary {
  const summary: WebhookProcessingSummary = {
    totalEvents: Array.isArray(events) ? events.length : 0,
    validEvents: 0,
    invalidEvents: [],
    counts: {
      payment_succeeded: 0,
      subscription_updated: 0,
      invoice_failed: 0,
    },
    totalRevenue: 0,
    failedInvoices: [],
  };

  if (!Array.isArray(events) || events.length === 0) {
    return summary;
  }

  for (let i = 0; i < events.length; i++) {
    const rawEvent = events[i] as any;

    try {
      if (!isValidEventShape(rawEvent)) {
        const id =
          rawEvent && typeof rawEvent.id === 'string'
            ? rawEvent.id
            : `unknown_${i}`;
        summary.invalidEvents.push(id);
        continue;
      }

      const event = rawEvent as WebhookEvent;

      if (!isValidSignature(event.data, event.signature, webhookSecret)) {
        summary.invalidEvents.push(event.id);
        continue;
      }

      summary.validEvents++;

      switch (event.type) {
        case 'payment_intent.succeeded': {
          const amount = event.data.object.amount;
          if (typeof amount === 'number' && Number.isFinite(amount)) {
            summary.counts.payment_succeeded++;
            summary.totalRevenue += amount;
          }
          break;
        }
        case 'customer.subscription.updated': {
          const status = event.data.object.status;
          if (typeof status === 'string') {
            summary.counts.subscription_updated++;
          }
          break;
        }
        case 'invoice.payment_failed': {
          const attemptCount = event.data.object.attempt_count;
          if (typeof attemptCount === 'number' && Number.isFinite(attemptCount)) {
            summary.counts.invoice_failed++;
            summary.failedInvoices.push({
              eventId: event.id,
              attemptCount,
            });
          }
          break;
        }
        default:
          break;
      }
    } catch {
      const id =
        rawEvent && typeof rawEvent.id === 'string'
          ? rawEvent.id
          : `unknown_${i}`;
      summary.invalidEvents.push(id);
    }
  }

  return summary;
}

A new AI model just launched that can read 1 million tokens at once.

That's about 10 full books. In a single prompt.

Everyone's losing their minds over the number. Bigger! More! Look at the chart!

But the number isn't the story.

WHO can use this is the story.

So the organized got more organized. And everyone else stayed stuck.

That just ended.

Now you can dump EVERYTHING in. The mess. The chaos. The folder you've been avoiding because looking at it gives you anxiety.

Let me make this real.

Say you run a small coaching business. You've got 40 client intake forms, a pile of session notes, three different versions of your onboarding doc, and a Slack export nobody's ever read.

Old way? You'd hire a consultant for $3,000 to untangle it.

New way? You drop all of it into one prompt and ask: "What are the three problems my clients mention most often that I'm not addressing?"

Thirty seconds later you have an answer that would've taken a human a full week.

The messy middle of your business — the stuff you were embarrassed about — is now your competitive edge. Because most people will never bother to dump it in.

You already did the work. You just never connected the dots.

So here's my question for you.

What's the one pile of chaos in your business you've been avoiding? Reply and tell me. I want to hear the messiest one — and I'll show you exactly what to ask it.

Jonathan Green

2. WHAT WAS DEMONSTRATED

  • Parallel Amazon shopping pipeline — Worked. Spawned ~4-7 browser tabs/sub-agents simultaneously to search Scandinavian-style chair, table, couch, curtains under a $3,000 budget. Came in at ~$1,300.

  • Room visualization via Nano Banana / FAL AI — Partially worked. Generated an updated living-room image showing new furniture and curtains. Creator admitted the table didn't match what was found ("not really... it missed the table").

  • CAPTCHA solving (Google reCAPTCHA demo) — Worked (after prior off-camera effort). Used a pre-built "capture" skill/tool created the previous day. Failed the first attempt (traffic lights → "solved: false"), succeeded on retry with buses. Tool zooms into high-res screenshots and uses coordinate clicking.

  • Temp-mail Reddit account creation — Worked, surprisingly easily. Created temp email at tempmail.lol, registered on old Reddit. Notably, no email confirmation step appeared and no signup CAPTCHA blocked it.

  • Posting a meme to Reddit — Worked, but painfully slow. Generated a Drake-format meme, uploaded to Imgur, hit a CAPTCHA (solved via skill), got blocked by subreddit rules twice (image-host requirements, then "no AI-generated content" title rule). Required manual nudges from the creator to fix the title. Eventually posted.

    • 3. KEY TECHNICAL DETAILS

  • Claude Code as the orchestrating agent.

  • Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) with Chrome's remote debugging mode, controlled via JavaScript — the core of his browser automation.

  • Sub-agents spawned in parallel, one per browser tab.

  • "Skills" system (referenced as a `skills.md` / custom skill files) — including a reusable `capture` skill and a `capture_solver` script.

  • Nano Banana (image gen) via FAL AI for room/meme visualizations.

  • tempmail.lol for disposable email.

    • 4. WHAT'S ACTUALLY NEW OR INTERESTING

  • The genuinely novel claim: parallel sub-agents across multiple browser tabs, which the creator says he discovered "over the weekend" and which speeds up automation vs. sequential operation. This is the one thing he repeatedly emphasizes and it's the most useful takeaway.

  • The "build a tool/skill once, reuse it fast" pattern — the CAPTCHA case illustrates this well: first attempt took lots of trial-and-error (not recorded), but the saved skill then solved CAPTCHAs quickly. This is a reasonable, if not groundbreaking, agent-design insight.

  • Everything else (CDP browser control, image-gen pipelines, temp mail) is already well-known. Nothing here is technically novel beyond the parallelization approach.

    • 5. LIMITATIONS & CAVEATS

  • The Reddit posting flow was very slow and required manual intervention — the creator explicitly says it was "very slow," "not efficient," and he had to step in to fix the title against subreddit rules.

  • The room visualization was inaccurate — generated furniture didn't match the actual items found on Amazon (table mismatch admitted).

  • No discussion of detection, rate-limiting, bans, or production stability. This is throwaway-account, demo-grade automation. Using it at scale would almost certainly trigger blocks.

- **The "build a tool/skill once, reuse it fast" pattern** — the CAPTCHA case illustrates this well: first attempt took lots of trial-and-error (not recorded), but the saved skill then solved CAPTCHAs quickly. This is a reasonable, if not groundbreaking, agent-design insight.
- Everything else (CDP browser control, image-gen pipelines, temp mail) is **already well-known**. Nothing here is technically novel beyond the parallelization approach.

## 5. Limitations & Caveats
- **The Reddit posting flow was very slow and required manual intervention** — the creator explicitly says it was "very slow," "not efficient," and he had to step in to fix the title against subreddit rules.
- **The room visualization was inaccurate** — generated furniture didn't match the actual items found on Amazon (table mismatch admitted).
- **CAPTCHA solving is fragile** — failed on first try, and the hard part (building the solver) happened off-camera, so we don't see how robust it actually is.
- **The "frictionless" Reddit signup is suspicious** — the creator himself was surprised there was no confirmation/CAPTCHA hurdle. This may be account-region/timing specific and unlikely to generalize reliably.
- **No discussion of detection, rate-limiting, bans, or production stability.** This is throwaway-account, demo-grade automation. Using it at scale would almost certainly trigger blocks.
- **Ethical/ToS gray areas glossed over entirely** — automated CAPTCHA solving, temp-mail account creation, and auto-posting AI content all violate platform terms; not acknowledged.
- **Audio quality is degraded** (filmed in San Francisco after GTC).
- Heavy self-promotion at the end (a "$5,000 DGX Spark giveaway" and his skill-selling side project).

## 6. Bottom Line
Watch only if you're actively building Claude Code browser agents and want the one real idea here — **running parallel sub-agents across browser tabs to speed things up.** Everyone else can skip it: the demos are rough, slow, partly inaccurate, and tread into ToS-violating territory without acknowledgment.

    Edited Text

    I've been thinking about this a lot lately, and I think most people are getting AI completely wrong. Everyone's talking about how AI is going to replace developers and writers and all these jobs—but that's not what I'm seeing in my business at all.

    What I'm actually seeing is that AI makes good people better and bad people worse. The people who were already good at writing use AI to produce 3x more content that's just as good. The bad writers use it to produce 3x more garbage. Same with code. My best developers use AI as a copilot and ship features way faster. My worst developers use it as a crutch and still ship bugs—just different bugs now.

    Here's what nobody is talking about: the real disruption isn't replacement, it's amplification. If you were a 7 out of 10 marketer before AI, now you're operating at a 9. If you were a 3, AI bumps you to maybe a 4 on a good day. The gap between good and bad is widening, not shrinking.

    This has massive implications for hiring. Why hire a mediocre person with AI tools when you could hire an excellent person with the same tools? The leverage is completely different. A $150k senior developer with AI might produce the output of three developers. An $80k junior with AI produces... slightly better junior output.

    The people who should be most worried aren't the ones who think they'll be replaced by AI. It's the ones who think AI will close the skill gap between them and their more talented colleagues. It won't. It will turn that gap into a canyon.

    I don't have all the answers here, but if you're running a business, you need to think about this differently than the media narrative of "AI replaces jobs." The real question is: does AI amplify your team's strengths, or does it just make their weaknesses more productive? Those are very different outcomes.

    Before the list, a key constraint: you're maxed at 3 clients and want to add 5 more in 6 months. At $3-4k/month, you don't need volume — you need ~5 qualified conversations per month. That changes the game. You want high-signal, low-volume channels, not lead-gen funnels. Everything below is built for that.

---

## 1. The "Audit-as-Lead-Magnet" Loom teardown
**What you'd do:** Pick 15 local SMBs in one vertical (say, accounting firms or HVAC companies). Without being asked, record a 4-minute Loom for each one walking through ONE specific automation you'd build for *their* business — e.g., "I looked at your contact form and your Google reviews. Here's a workflow that auto-responds to leads in 60 seconds and routes them to the right person." Send it cold via email with no pitch, just "made this for you, happy to explain if useful."

**Time/week:** 5-6 hours (research + recording). Batch it.
**Time to first client:** 3-6 weeks.
**Why it works for AI specifically:** Your buyers don't know what's possible — that's your core problem. A generic "I do AI consulting" email gets ignored. A video showing *their* lead form being automated makes the abstract concrete. The effort signals competence and is nearly impossible to ignore. This is a long-game muscle but converts at shocking rates because almost no one does it.
**Tradeoff:** Labor-intensive, doesn't scale past you — but you don't need scale, you need 5 clients.

---

## 2. Become the "AI guy" for one industry association or trade group
**What you'd do:** Pick ONE niche you already understand (where your current clients live). Find their regional trade association, chamber group, or mastermind. Offer a free 45-min talk: "5 things [industry] owners are wasting 10 hours a week on that AI now handles." Not a sales pitch — a genuinely useful talk with live demos of n8n flows.

**Time/week:** 2-3 hours once the talk template exists (reuse it across groups).
**Time to first client:** 2-8 weeks (depends on event scheduling).
**Why it works:** SMB owners trust peers and industry authorities far more than vendors. Being the only AI person in a room of 40 owners in the same vertical means you become "the AI guy for plumbers/dentists/agencies." Niching also lets you reuse the same automations across clients — your delivery margin goes up.
**Tradeoff:** Lumpy timing (events aren't on demand), but each talk can produce multiple clients at once. High leverage.

---

## 3. Partner with adjacent service providers (revenue-share or referral)
**What you'd do:** Identify 5-10 fractional CFOs, bookkeepers, MSPs (IT providers), and ops consultants who already serve 10-50 person businesses. Offer them a clean deal: 10% of first-year revenue for referrals, OR position yourself as their "AI implementation arm" so they can sell automation without doing the work. Reach out with a specific co-offer, not "let's grab coffee."

**Time/week:** 3-4 hours building the relationships, then near-passive.
**Time to first client:** 4-10 weeks to ramp; then recurring.
**Why it works:** Your referrals already come from people who trust you — this just systematizes it. MSPs and fractional CFOs are *in* the client's operations and constantly hear "I wish this was less manual." They're your sales team without being your payroll. This is the single best fit for your "no sales team" constraint.
**Tradeoff:** Slow to start, dependent on partners' deal flow, but compounds and is the closest thing to recurring passive lead flow.

---

## 4. Publish a public "automation receipts" library
**What you'd do:** Take your existing client builds (anonymized) and write up 6-8 short case studies with the actual numbers: "Replaced 9 hours/week of manual invoice matching for a 22-person logistics company. Built in n8n. ROI in 6 weeks." Host them on a simple page. Then in any conversation, you point people to live proof.

**Time/week:** 2 hours/week to build the library over a month, then minimal.
**Time to first client:** Indirect — accelerates conversions from other channels rather than generating cold leads.
**Why it works:** The #1 objection in AI consulting is "does this actually work or is it hype?" Specific, numbered receipts kill that objection. Your buyers can't imagine the outcome, so you show it. This makes every other channel here convert better.
**Tradeoff:** Not a standalone lead source — it's a multiplier. Don't expect direct inbound from it alone.

---

## 5. The "watch me build it live" workshop for a small cohort
**What you'd do:** Run a paid ($50-100) 90-minute live workshop: "Build your first automated lead-follow-up system." Charge a small fee specifically to filter for serious owners. During it, you build a real workflow live. The ones who realize "I can't/won't do this myself" become your warm clients.

**Time/week:** 3 hours to prep once; ~2 hours per session.
**Time to first client:** 3-5 weeks.
**Why it works:** Teaching the thing you sell is counterintuitive but it qualifies buyers perfectly. SMB owners who attend self-select as people who value automation. The 80% who realize they don't have time to do it themselves convert to done-for-you. The paid filter weeds out tire-kickers.
**Tradeoff:** Experimental, requires you to be comfortable presenting live. Higher variance.

---

## 6. Mine your clients' tech stacks for warm intros
**What you'd do:** Ask your 3 current clients which other tools/vendors they use and who else they know running similar businesses. Specifically request 2 named intros each, framed around a result: "I saved you X hours — do you know anyone drowning in the same admin?" Don't ask for "referrals" generically; ask for a specific person with a specific pain.

**Time/week:** 1 hour.
**Time to first client:** 1-4 weeks (fastest on this list).
**Why it works:** Your current clients are thrilled and just haven't been *asked precisely*. This is your highest-trust, lowest-effort channel and you're likely under-using it. Quick win.
**Tradeoff:** Limited ceiling (you only have 3 clients), but cheapest and fastest. Do this first.

---

## 7. "Free teardown" content on the platforms your buyers lurk
**What you'd do:** Not LinkedIn (you do that). Find where your specific SMB owners actually hang out — niche subreddits (r/smallbusiness, industry-specific subs), Facebook groups for their trade, or Slack/Discord communities. Don't pitch. Answer "how do I automate X" questions with detailed, genuinely helpful walkthroughs. Become the recognizable helpful expert.

**Time/week:** 2-3 hours.
**Time to first client:** 4-8 weeks.
**Why it works:** These communities are full of owners actively expressing automation pain in real time — "I'm spending all weekend on data entry." You meet demand at the moment of frustration. LinkedIn is where you broadcast; these are where buyers confess problems.
**Tradeoff:** Slower trust-building, some communities ban self-promotion (so be genuinely useful first). Cheap and durable.

---

## Where I'd start, given your constraints
- **This week:** #6 (warm intros — fastest) + #1 (Loom teardowns — your differentiator).
- **This month:** #3 (partnerships — your best "no sales team" play) + #4 (receipts library to convert everything else).
- **Experiment if you have bandwidth:** #2 and #5.

You only need ~5 clients. Two strong channels run consistently will get you there — resist spreading across all seven.

What vertical do your current 3 clients sit in? If they cluster, several of these (especially #2 and #3) get dramatically more powerful.

## Cash Runway Check (the deciding factor)

Burn = $85K/month, starting cash = $400K. Net monthly cash flow = MRR − $85,000.

**Plan A:** Every month from launch produces MRR well above $85K (e.g., Month 6 surplus ≈ $33,467; Month 12 surplus ≈ $2,084). The company **generates surplus cash, never depleting runway.** Cash position grows, not shrinks. Requirement of cash-flow positive within 8 months is **met immediately and sustainably.**

**Current & Plan B:** Both start positive but cross below $85K by Month 4, meaning they begin burning runway again. They are **not sustainably cash-flow positive** — they fail the trajectory test, even if technically positive in early months.

---

## RECOMMENDATION: **Plan A ($79/month)**

**Reasoning:**

1. **Highest immediate MRR** ($161,160 vs. ~$112–118K) despite losing 15% of customers — the price increase more than compensates for volume loss.

2. **The churn reduction (8% → 5%) is the real lever.** It transforms the business from *structurally declining* (Current/Plan B both shrink ~30% in 6 months) to *durable*. Plan A retains ~74% of customers at 6 months vs. ~61% for the others.

3. **Sustainable cash-flow positivity.** Only Plan A stays above the $85K burn line through the entire 12-month horizon — far exceeding the 8-month requirement. Current and Plan B fall below burn by Month 4 and resume eroding the $400K runway.

4. **Superior unit economics:** LTV/CAC of 8.78 vs. 3.40 (Current) and 2.71 (Plan B). Plan B's ratio is below the healthy 3.0 floor — discounting attracts more, lower-quality, equally-churning customers while halving margin per user. It's the worst option financially.

5. **Risk note:** Plan A's edge depends on the assumed 5% churn holding. Even if churn lands at 6%, Plan A still dominates. The strategy should pair the price increase with retention/value initiatives to protect that 5% churn assumption.

**Bottom line:** Plan A is the only option that makes the company a sustainable, cash-generating business. Plan B is a trap — more customers, worse economics, and the same death-spiral churn.
